title: FDA Letter to Industry Concerning Liquid Vitamin D Dietary Supplements
authors: US Food and Drug Administration; signed by Joshua M. Sharfstein, Principal Deputy Commissioner of Food and Drugs
journal: US Food and Drug Administration, Dietary Supplements Guidance Documents and Regulatory Information, June 2010 (archived FDA page, last updated 26 November 2014)
result: FDA was concerned that some liquid vitamin D products for infants are sold with droppers that can hold considerably more liquid vitamin D than an infant should receive, so that caregivers could give an unsafe dose by mistake. The letter describes vitamin D toxicity: initial symptoms usually associated with high serum calcium include weakness, fatigue, lassitude, headache, nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea; mental status changes and coma may develop; cardiac arrhythmias may ensue; renal function may be affected early; prolonged hypercalcaemia can lead to soft tissue deposition of calcium, favoured in the kidney; osteomalacia may occur; if caught early, treatment may completely reverse the symptoms, but residual sequelae may include permanent renal impairment and osteoporosis. The letter text carries no date; the FDA guidance index lists it as June 2010. FDA recommended that droppers be clearly and accurately marked at 400 units and that droppers for infant products hold no more than 400 units.
